prize_parts.citation: for the development of lipid nanoparticles that deliver nucleic-acid medicines into cells

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a molecular-design solution to a problem that blocked a whole class of drugs: how to get a large, charged, fragile nucleic acid into the cytosol. The chemistry is real and specific (pKa-tuned ionizable headgroups, lipid polymorphism and endosomal escape, controlled self-assembly by rapid mixing), and the outcome is demonstrated at scale, with approved siRNA therapy and billions of mRNA vaccine doses. Few candidates on the shortlist combine a clearly chemical mechanism, independent replication by many groups and a direct change in what clinicians can do. Cullis represents the formulation and ionizable-lipid line from Vancouver; Langer represents the broader delivery-materials concept and combinatorial lipid discovery that made the platform general. I think this is both timely and overdue as a chemistry prize, distinct from the 2023 Medicine prize, which recognised nucleoside modification and not the vehicle.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list has six names and the decisive contributions are spread over formulation chemistry (Cullis, Hope, Madden), the first clinically validated siRNA products (MacLachlan) and lipidoid and combinatorial discovery (Anderson, Langer). Any two- or three-person cut leaves out people who did essential work, and part of the translational chemistry sits in industry and is partly proprietary. There is also a reasonable argument that the nearby 2023 Medicine prize already covered the mRNA vaccine story, so a delivery prize may look derivative, and that I am drawn to this candidate because it sits close to my own translational interests.

responses.point: Sparr ranked ionizable lipid nanoparticles second and proposed Cullis, Hope and Madden as the foundational formulation trio, arguing that the physical chemistry of lipid phase behaviour and pH-dependent charge is the core, and that translation was industrial and partly proprietary.
responses.response: I agree with Emma on the science: the membrane and colloid chemistry is the heart of this discovery, and her reading of the lipid physical chemistry is sharper than mine. Where I differ is on the third name. Hope and Madden were essential to the early Vancouver work, but a prize that credits only that group misses the point that delivery became general, and not a single-lipid trick, through combinatorial lipid design. That is why I keep Langer alongside Cullis. I accept that Hope or Madden could reasonably replace Langer if the committee wants to stay strictly within the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing line, and I would like to hear her view on whether the lipidoid strand is chemically decisive or only supportive.

responses.point: Linke ranked halide perovskites first, citing the jump from a few percent to over 25 percent efficiency in about a decade, a clear physical picture and a new solution-processed semiconductor class, while accepting that stability, lead content and deployment remain open.
responses.response: I take the scientific breadth of perovskites seriously, and the Miyasaka-Park-Snaith chain of credit is cleaner than for lipid nanoparticles. But Heiner's own maturity caveat cuts hard here: after fifteen years there is still no commercially deployed perovskite module, whereas ionizable lipid nanoparticles are already in approved drugs and have been tested at population scale. If we weigh demonstrated impact together with originality, I think the lipid delivery case is at least as strong, and the tidier attribution for perovskites does not by itself outweigh a lack of proven consequences. I would also question whether the committee would rather wait for a stability answer.

responses.point: Aqvist ranked Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first as a clean two-person methodological invention with decades of use, and placed targeted protein degradation second as a new drug modality whose clinical proof is still pending.
responses.response: I agree with Johan that Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli are a serious second choice, and I also ranked degradation second, so on that point we are close. His maturity reservation about PROTACs is the same as mine and is the main reason I place lipid nanoparticles ahead of them. On Car-Parrinello, I accept that the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and that the method is foundational, but I am not yet convinced it changed what researchers outside theory can do, and the argument that Born-Oppenheimer MD has partly displaced the original scheme weakens the case for lasting impact. I would ask him which result in the field depends specifically on the fictitious-dynamics formulation.

responses.point: Chabes ranked massively parallel sequencing first, stressing that reversible-terminator chemistry is the foundation of modern genomics, while acknowledging a contested allocation between Solexa chemistry, pyrosequencing and Ju's terminators.
responses.response: Andrei's argument is strong on impact and on the concrete nucleotide chemistry, and I ranked sequencing fourth myself. My hesitation is the one he names: three credits cannot capture the reversible terminators, clustering and the 454 line, and the committee may see this as instrumentation. I would put it on par with lipid nanoparticles for impact but behind them for clarity of a single molecular-design insight. I would find it helpful if he could say which two names he considers non-negotiable, because that decides whether this is a viable configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing line (Cullis, Hope, Madden) or the lipidoid and combinatorial line (Anderson, Langer) is the chemically decisive one.
Whether the committee will see a delivery-vehicle prize as too close to the 2023 Medicine prize.
How much weight to give clinical maturity: lipid nanoparticles are approved, PROTACs are not yet, and perovskites are not commercially deployed.
I am working from recalled history of who invented which lipid generation and have not verified the priority details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no known connection to the Vancouver, MIT or Alnylam groups. My translational and biomaterials interests mean I am sympathetic to delivery technologies, which I have tried to state openly.
